'''James K. Freericks''' (born 1963) is an American physicist who holds the McDevitt chair in physics at Georgetown University. He has worked in fields of [[condensed matter physics]], [[mathematical physics]], [[atomic physics]], nonequilibrium physics, [[quantum computation]], and quantum mechanics pedagogy. His [[massive open online course]] (MOOC) "Quantum Mechanics for Everyone" was ranked #3 in the world by Class Central in 2024.

== Early life and education ==
He was born in [[Paramus, New Jersey]], to parents Mary and Charles Freericks. He attended Spring Valley Elementary School, Memorial Elementary School, East Brook Middle School and [[Paramus High School]], graduating in 1981.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Delphian |date=1 May 1980 |publisher=Paramus High School |volume=XXI |location=Paramus, New Jersey |pages=121, 152, 158}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/1981_20191215/page/10/mode/2up?q=%22jim+freericks%22+ |title=Delphian |date=1 May 1981 |publisher=Paramus High School |volume=XXII |location=Paramus, New Jersey |pages=10, 44–47, 73–76}}</ref> He was influenced by his uncle, Peter Avakian, a research physicist at [[DuPont]], to enter the field of physics.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Avakian |first1=Peter |title=Modern Fluoropolymers: High Performance Polymers for Diverse Applications |last2=Starkweather, Jr. |first2=Howard W. |date=9 September 1997 |page=91 |chapter=High Performance Polymers for Diverse Applications}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Avakian |first1=Peter |title=Dielectric Spectroscopy of Polymeric Materials: Fundamentals and Applications |last2=Starkweather, Jr. |first2=Howard W. |last3=Fontanella |first3=John J. |last4=Wintersgill |first4=Mary C. |date=1997 |publisher=American Chemical Society |editor-last=Runt |editor-first=James P. |location=Washington, DC |chapter=Dielectric Properties of Fluoropolymers |editor-last2=Fitzgerald |editor-first2=John J.}}</ref>

In 1981 he entered [[Princeton University]] as a physics major, graduating in 1985.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Nassau Herald: Princeton University, Class of 1985 |date=2 May 1985 |publisher=Princeton University |volume=CVII |page=118 |chapter=James K. Freericks}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1981-1987, 1981-1987 - Finding Aids |url=https://findingaids.princeton.edu/catalog/AC115_c0073?onlineToggle=false |access-date=2024-12-05 |website=Princeton University Commencement Records, 1748-2024}}</ref> His senior thesis, ''[https://catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/9941223483506421 Time Reversal-Invariance Tests in Muon Capture]'', explored whether one can use [[muon capture]] in spin-polarized [[Exotic atom|muonic hydrogen]] to examine time reversal invariance violation (equivalent to [[CP violation]]); he was advised by physicists Frank Calaprice and [[Sam Treiman]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Freericks |first=James K. |url=https://catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/9941223483506421 |title=Time Reversal-invariance Tests in Muon Capture |date=1985 |publisher=Department of Physics, Princeton University |location=}}</ref> He also worked at the [[Thomas J. Watson Research Center|Thomas J. Watson Research Center (IBM Yorktown)]] as a summer student on their [[Neutrino|neutrino mass]] experiment, examining weak-interaction contributions to [[beta decay]] and how accurately the retarding grid will measure the final-state energy.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Clark |first1=G.J. |url=https://inis.iaea.org/search/searchsinglerecord.aspx?recordsFor=SingleRecord&RN=19021322 |title=The IBM neutrino-mass experiment |last2=Frisch |first2=M.A. |last3=Chaudhari |first3=P. |last4=Bregman |first4=M.F. |date=1985 |publisher=World Scientific Pub Co |isbn=978-9971-978-46-4 |location=United States}}</ref> He graduated from Princeton [[summa cum laude]], was elected to [[Phi Beta Kappa]], and won the [https://nikkeivoice.ca/treasures-from-the-nikkei-national-museum-shuichi-kusaka-memorial-fund-brochure/ Kusaka Memorial prize] in physics. At the [[University of California, Berkeley]], he initially started as a [[String theory|string theorist]], but changed to work in [[condensed matter physics]] with [[Leopoldo Máximo Falicov|Leo Falicov]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Freericks |first=J. K. |date=1989 |title=Dephasing effects in a two-dimensional magnetic-breakdown linked-orbit network: Magnesium |url=https://journals.aps.org/prb/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevB.39.5678 |journal=Physical Review B |volume=39 |issue=9 |pages=5678–5683 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.39.5678|pmid=9948980 |bibcode=1989PhRvB..39.5678F |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Freericks |first=James Knox |url=https://search.library.berkeley.edu/discovery/fulldisplay?docid=alma991077465099706532&context=L&vid=01UCS_BER:UCB&lang=en&search_scope=DN_and_CI&adaptor=Local%20Search%20Engine&tab=Default_UCLibrarySearch&query=any,contains,Freericks%20dissertation&offset=0 |title=Electron Correlations in Solid-State Physics |date=1 January 1991 |publisher=PhD Dissertation, The University of California, Berkeley |location=Berkeley, California}}</ref> His 1991 dissertation was focused on small-cluster [[exact diagonalization]] studies, examining magnetism and symmetry properties.<ref name=":2" /> He was a [[National Science Foundation]] graduate fellowship awardee and a two-time Department of Education fellowship awardee.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Freericks |first1=J. K. |last2=Falicov |first2=L. M. |last3=Rokhsar |first3=D. S. |date=1991-07-15 |title=Exact solutions of frustrated ordinary and chiral eight-site Hubbard models |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevB.44.1458 |journal=Physical Review B |language=en |volume=44 |issue=4 |pages=1458–1474 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.44.1458 |pmid=9999678 |bibcode=1991PhRvB..44.1458F |issn=0163-1829}}</ref> He then went to the [[Institute for Theoretical Physics (Santa Barbara)|Institute for Theoretical Physics]] in Santa Barbara (1991–93) as a postdoctoral fellow working with physicist [[Douglas James Scalapino|Douglas Scalapino]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Freericks |first1=J. K. |last2=Scalapino |first2=D. J. |date=1994-03-01 |title=Weak-coupling expansions for the attractive Holstein and Hubbard models |journal=Physical Review B |volume=49 |issue=9 |pages=6368–6371 |doi=10.1103/physrevb.49.6368 |issn=0163-1829 |pmid=10011634|arxiv=cond-mat/9308024 |bibcode=1994PhRvB..49.6368F }}</ref> It is there that he started working in [[dynamical mean-field theory]] and began a long-standing collaboration with Mark Jarrell, then at the [[University of Cincinnati]].<ref name="tandfonline.com">{{Cite journal |last1=Pruschke |first1=Th. |last2=Jarrell |first2=M. |last3=Freericks |first3=J. K. |date=1 January 1995 |title=Anomalous normal-state properties of high- T c superconductors: intrinsic properties of strongly correlated electron systems? |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00018739500101526 |journal=Advances in Physics |language= |volume=44 |issue=2 |pages=187–210 |doi=10.1080/00018739500101526 |arxiv=supr-con/9502001 |bibcode=1995AdPhy..44..187P |issn=0001-8732}}</ref> His second postdoctoral fellowship was at the [[University of California, Davis]] (1993–94), working with Richard Scalettar.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Freericks |first=J. K. |date=1994-07-01 |title=Conserving approximations for the attractive Holstein and Hubbard models |url=https://journals.aps.org/prb/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevB.50.403 |journal=Physical Review B |language=en |volume=50 |issue=1 |pages=403–417 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.50.403 |pmid=9974557 |arxiv=cond-mat/9402029 |bibcode=1994PhRvB..50..403F |issn=0163-1829}}</ref>

== Work as a physicist ==
He arrived at [[Georgetown University]] in 1994 as an assistant professor, promoted to associate professor in 1998, and full professor in 2002. He was made the inaugural Robert L. McDevitt, K.S.G., K.C.H.S and Catherine H. McDevitt, L.C.H.S. Chair in physics in 2010.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=McDevitt Chair in Physics |url=https://physics.georgetown.edu/mcdevitt-chair-physics/ |access-date=2024-12-02 |website=Department of Physics |language=en-US}}</ref> He was awarded the [[Oak Ridge Associated Universities]] Junior Faculty Enhancement Award (1995) and the [[Office of Naval Research]] Young Investigator Award in 1996.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Jim Freericks 2023 Election Bio |url=https://www.aapt.org/aboutaapt/Jim-Freericks-2023-Election-Bio.cfm |access-date=2024-12-02 |website=American Association of Physics Teachers}}</ref> He is a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (2006), having served as the treasurer and secretary of the Division of Computational Physics from 2012 to 2017.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Physics - James K. Freericks |url=https://physics.aps.org/authors/james_k_freericks |website=American Physical Society |language=}}</ref> He was the Councillor for the Division of Computational Physics and the Topical Group on Big Data from 2020 to 2023.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Division, Forum, and Section Councilors |url=https://res.cloudinary.com/apsphysics/image/upload/2021-01_vvaktp.pdf |journal=APS News |volume=30 |issue=1 |page=2}}</ref> He is currently the treasurer of the [[American Association of Physics Teachers]] and is the section representative of its Chesapeake section.<ref name=":1" /> He became a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 2018.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2018-11-30 |title=2018 AAAS Fellows approved by the AAAS Council |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.362.6418.1010 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=362 |issue=6418 |pages=1010–1013 |doi=10.1126/science.362.6418.1010 |bibcode=2018Sci...362.1010. |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He was named a Slater lecturer at the [[University of Florida]] in 2019.<ref>{{Cite web |title=People – Quantum Information Systems |url=https://faculty.eng.ufl.edu/quantum-information-systems/people/ |website=The University of Florida |language=}}</ref> He has served on the editorial boards of the ''Nature'' journal ''[[Scientific Reports]]'', [[Symmetry (journal)|''Symmetry'']] and the ''[[American Journal of Physics]]''.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Editorial Board for Section 'Physics' |url=https://www.mdpi.com/journal/symmetry/sectioneditors/physics?page_no=2 |website=Symmetry |language=}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=AJP- Editorial Staff |url=https://www.aapt.org/Publications/AJP/About/editors_and_staff.cfm |access-date=2024-12-04 |website=www.aapt.org}}</ref>

His early research focused on small cluster calculations for [[strongly correlated material]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Freericks |first=James K. |title=Annotated Publication List |url=https://site.physics.georgetown.edu/~jkf/annotate.html |website=Georgetown University Department of Physics}}</ref> He then moved into the electron-phonon problem, examining [[Vertex function|vertex corrections]]. He has worked on two projects with mathematical physicist [[Elliott H. Lieb|Elliott Lieb]] of Princeton, and other mathematical physics problems.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Freericks |first1=James K. |last2=Lieb |first2=Elliott H. |last3=Ueltschi |first3=Daniel |date=2002-03-11 |title=Phase Separation Due to Quantum Mechanical Correlations |url=https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/phase-separation-due-to-quantum-mechanical-correlations |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=88 |issue=10 |pages=1064011–1064014 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.88.106401 |issn=0031-9007 |pmid=11909377|arxiv=cond-mat/0110251 |bibcode=2002PhRvL..88j6401F }}</ref> He was one of the pioneers in [[dynamical mean-field theory]], working primarily on transport and other [[Frequency response|response functions]].<ref name="tandfonline.com"/> His first book, ''Transport in Multilayered Nanostructures: The Dynamical Mean-Field Theory Approach'', won the 2009 [[Alpha Sigma Nu]] best book prize for physical science.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Freericks |first=James K. |title=Transport in Multilayered Nanostructures: The Dynamical Mean-field Theory Approach |date=2009 |publisher=Imperial College Press, World Scientific Publishing |isbn=978-1-78326-857-3 |edition= |location=Covent Garden}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=19 January 2018 |title=Past Winners [1979-2018] |url=https://www.alphasigmanu.org/images/uploads/resources/Past_Winners_of_Book_Awards_2018.pdf |website=Alpha Sigma Nu Book Awards}}</ref> He generalized [[dynamical mean-field theory]] into nonequilibrium, and focused on examining [[Pump–probe microscopy|pump-probe]] experiments.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Freericks |first1=J. K. |last2=Turkowski |first2=V. M. |last3=Zlatić |first3=V. |date=2006-12-29 |title=Nonequilibrium Dynamical Mean-Field Theory |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.97.266408 |journal=Physical Review Letters |language=en |volume=97 |issue=26 |article-number=266408 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.97.266408 |pmid=17280443 |arxiv=cond-mat/0607053 |bibcode=2006PhRvL..97z6408F |issn=0031-9007}}</ref> He was part of the [[DARPA]] [[optical lattice]] emulator program, which initiated his work with [[Ion trap|ion trap simulators]], including the first simulation in a [[Penning trap]] with hundreds of qubits.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cho |first=Adrian |date=2008-04-18 |title=The Mad Dash to Make Light Crystals |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.320.5874.312 |journal=Science |volume=320 |issue=5874 |pages=312–313 |doi=10.1126/science.320.5874.312|pmid=18420913 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Britton |first1=Joseph W. |last2=Sawyer |first2=Brian C. |last3=Keith |first3=Adam C. |last4=Wang |first4=C.-C. Joseph |last5=Freericks |first5=James K. |last6=Uys |first6=Hermann |last7=Biercuk |first7=Michael J. |last8=Bollinger |first8=John J. |date=2 April 2012 |title=Engineered two-dimensional Ising interactions in a trapped-ion quantum simulator with hundreds of spins |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature10981 |journal=Nature |language= |volume=484 |issue=7395 |pages=489–492 |doi=10.1038/nature10981 |pmid=22538611 |arxiv=1204.5789 |bibcode=2012Natur.484..489B |issn=0028-0836}}</ref> More recently, he focused on working on how [[quantum computing]] can be used to simulate real science problems (including a damped-driven simulation of 1000 Trotter steps) and how to re-envision how quantum mechanics is taught.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Rost |first1=Brian |title=Long-Time Error-Mitigating Simulation of Open Quantum Systems on Near Term Quantum Computers |date=2021 |arxiv=2108.01183 |last2=Del Re |first2=Lorenzo |last3=Earnest |first3=Nathan |last4=Kemper |first4=Alexander F. |last5=Jones |first5=Barbara |last6=Freericks |first6=James K.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Freericks |first1=J. K. |last2=Cutler |first2=D. |last3=Kruse |first3=A. |last4=Vieira |first4=L. B. |date=2019-05-01 |title=Teaching Quantum Mechanics to Over 28,000 Nonscientists |url=https://pubs.aip.org/pte/article/57/5/326/1016268/Teaching-Quantum-Mechanics-to-Over-28-000 |journal=The Physics Teacher |language=en |volume=57 |issue=5 |pages=326–329 |doi=10.1119/1.5098924 |arxiv=1712.02660 |bibcode=2019PhTea..57..326F |issn=0031-921X}}</ref>

== MOOC, Quantum Mechanics for Everyone ==
In 2017, he released the [[Massive open online course|MOOC]] Quantum Mechanics for Everyone.<ref>{{Cite web |title=GeorgetownX: Quantum Mechanics for Everyone |url=https://www.edx.org/learn/quantum-physics-mechanics/georgetown-university-quantum-mechanics-for-everyone?correlationId=9e7cbd8d-19bc-45e8-966f-c5c5b588f495 |website=edX |language=en}}</ref> He teaches the ideas behind [[superposition]], measurement, [[Entanglement distillation|entanglement]], complementarity, and tagging (a reversible way to create entangled states). The class is based on the ideas of theoretical physicists [[Richard Feynman]] and [[Daniel F. Styer|Daniel Styer]], and requires no more advanced math or physics than what is covered at the high school level. It was a finalist for the 2018 edX award.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=14 September 2018 |title=The 2018 Best edX Instructors |url=https://iblnews.org/the-2018-best-edx-org-instructors/ |website=IBL News |language=}}</ref> It is ranked number 3 in the top 250 MOOCs of all time by class central.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Class Central's Best Online Courses of All Time (2021 Edition) |url=https://www.classcentral.com/report/top-moocs-2021-edition/ |website=Class Central: The Report}}</ref> Freericks has taught over 60,000 students through the MOOC.<ref>{{Cite web |title=GeorgetownX: Quantum Mechanics for Everyone |url=https://www.edx.org/learn/quantum-physics-mechanics/georgetown-university-quantum-mechanics-for-everyone |access-date=2024-12-05 |website=edX |language=en}}</ref> He has two other MOOCs---one on mathematical methods and one on quantum mechanics—both college-level courses closely paralleling his offerings at Georgetown University.<ref>{{Cite web |title=GeorgetownX: Quantum Mechanics |url=https://www.edx.org/learn/quantum-physics-mechanics/georgetown-university-quantum-mechanics |access-date=2024-12-05 |website=edX |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=GeorgetownX: Mathematical and Computational Methods |url=https://www.edx.org/learn/math/georgetown-university-mathematical-and-computational-methods |access-date=2024-12-05 |website=edX |language=en}}</ref> He teaches them annually, and the math methods course was a finalist for the 2023 edX award for innovation in online teaching.<ref>{{Cite web |last=edX |title=Celebrating the 2023 edX Prize Finalists for Innovation in Online Teaching |url=https://press.edx.org/2023-edx-prize-finalists |access-date=2024-12-02 |website=press.edx.org |language=en}}</ref>

== Book, ''Quantum Mechanics Done Right'' ==
After the first cohort of students took the MOOC "Quantum Mechanics for Everyone," there was demand for more materials.<ref>{{Cite web |title=James K. Freericks Bio and Featured Works |url=https://gufaculty360.georgetown.edu/s/contact/00336000014RbYDAA0/james-freericks |website=Georgetown360}}</ref> From a physics colleague, Wes Mathews, Freericks learned about the [[Erwin Schrödinger|Schroedinger]] factorization method and how quantum mechanics can be taught with a more algebraic focus rather than a differential equation approach.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Freericks |first1=James K. |last2=Mathews Jr. |first2=Wesley N. |date=2 April 2023 |title=Continuum Energy Eigenstates via the Factorization Method |journal=Symmetry |language= |volume=15 |issue=4 |page=797 |doi=10.3390/sym15040797 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2302.10365 |bibcode=2023Symm...15..797F |issn=2073-8994}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=In memory of Wesley N. Mathews Jr. (1937 – 2022) |url=https://physics.georgetown.edu/in-memory-of-wesley-n-mathews-jr-1937-2022/ |website=Georgetown University Department of Physics |language=en-US}}</ref> His book ''Quantum Mechanics Done Right: The Shortest Path from Novice to Researcher,'' will appear in 2025.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Weitzman |last2=Freericks |date=1 September 2018 |title=Calculating spherical harmonics without derivatives |url=http://www.icmp.lviv.ua/journal/zbirnyk.95/33002/abstract.html |journal=Condensed Matter Physics |volume=21 |issue=3 |article-number=33002 |doi=10.5488/CMP.21.33002|arxiv=1805.12125 |bibcode=2018CMPh...2133002W }}</ref> Freericks focuses on conceptual ideas and quantum reasoning first (as discussed in the first four modules of his MOOC), before developing conventional topics in quantum mechanics using unconventional methods.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Quantum Mechanics for Everyone |url=https://www.my-mooc.com/en/mooc/quantum-mechanics-for-everyone |access-date=2024-12-05 |website=My Mooc |language=en}}</ref> Freericks developed these materials with undergraduates, high school students, and citizen scientists, publishing multiple papers on these topics for the book.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Link to work with citizen scientists and undergraduate scientists |url=https://quantum.georgetown.domains/research.html |website=Research on Quantum Mechanics Pedagogy, Georgetown University |language=}}</ref>
